title: Client-side optimistic reservation protocol for dedup-safe billing
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem:
Customers that use at-least-once delivery (client retries or network timeouts) can incur duplicate billed tokens when the server replays or re-processes a request. Existing idempotency solutions (server-side dedupe tables keyed by idempotency-key) work but have two practical problems we see in production: 1) long-lived dedupe state retention for high-client-volume keys becomes expensive; 2) client libraries across ecosystems fail to provide stable idempotency keys, leading to incomplete coverage.

Proposal (Sketch): Client-side optimistic reservation protocol. Instead of immediately committing billing on request receipt, the platform accepts a short-lived "reservation" that temporarily earmarks billing units. Reservations are created with a client-provided monotonic reservation-id (optional header X-Res-Id) + client-epoch pair, and a TTL (e.g., 30s). The request proceeds normally; when a final response is generated the server converts the reservation into a finalized invoice item. If the client retries with the same reservation-id within the TTL, the runtime recognizes the reservation and returns the cached finalization state (or a redirect to the canonical response) without double-charging.

Key behaviors:
- Reservation creation is cheap and idempotent: a create call either inserts a reservation row or returns the existing reservation metadata (reservation_id, created_at, ttl). The reservation by itself does not increment the usage ledger permanently.
- Finalize path uses compare-and-set against reservation state (pending -> finalized) and records a finalization receipt containing a canonical response-hash and sequence counter. Multiple finalizes for the same reservation are suppressed via CAS.
- Expiry reconciliation: expired reservations are garbage-collected by background sweeps and periodic reconciliation that reclaims orphaned reserved credits and converts them back to available quota. A reclamation job also cross-checks against downstream billing ledger to detect leaks.

Why this is different from a plain idempotency-key approach:
- Moves short-term state into a dedicated reservation lifecycle with explicit TTL and GC semantics instead of unbounded dedupe rows.
- Enables clients to avoid providing perfectly stable idempotency keys: they only need to retry within the reservation TTL to get dedupe guarantees.
- Opens the door to optimistic soft-crediting for quotas (allow a request to proceed while holding a cheap reservation token rather than doing heavy-weight ledger writes up-front).

Implementation notes (high-level):
- Reservation store: strongly consistent distribution with per-customer shard key. Implementation candidate: Postgres sharded by customer_id with an index on (customer_id, reservation_id) and a TTL column for fast GC OR a small in-memory LRU + durable append-log for longer tails.
- Finalization: single-row CAS (UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'pending') to transition to 'finalized' and write final_receipt_id. For high-throughput customers we will batch finalize receipts into a per-customer commit stream to amortize DB overhead.
- Quota/billing interaction: reservation consumes a soft-availability token. Finalize converts soft token -> hard billed charge against the consumption ledger. Reclamation controller is responsible for publishing negative adjustments for expired reservations when necessary.
- Telemetry: reservation-create, reservation-finalize, reservation-expire, reservation-gc, reservation-leak-detection metrics; histogram of reservation TTL usage; duplicate-finalize attempts counter.

Tradeoffs and Risks:
- Complexity: introduces a new lease lifecycle and GC surface. Requires robust reconciliation to avoid long-lived leakage of quota.
- Latency impact: reservation create adds 1 small write on hot path. We will micro-optimize to make this <1ms for cached reservation store and <5ms worst-case.
- Edge cases: clients that use multiple distinct reservation-ids per retry will not get dedupe benefit. We need clear SDK guidance and examples.
- Backwards compatibility: provided as opt-in; legacy idempotency behavior remains for clients that do not opt in.

Rollout Plan:
1) Implement feature-flagged server-side reservation store + finalize flow behind FF:metering.reservation. SDKs for Node/Python to add X-Res-Id helper.
2) Internal dogfood with Redwood Console and a small set of early-adopter customers (10% traffic shard).
3) Monitor duplicate-rate and reservation-leak metrics for 2 weeks; enable GC aggressiveness adjustments.
4) Gradually ramp to more customers and bake into default SDKs.

Acceptance criteria:
- Duplicate billing incidents for feature-flagged requests reduced by >90% in dogfood shard vs baseline.
- Reservation GC reclaims >99.9% of expired reservations within 24h in production tests.
- Latency p95 of request hot-path change <3ms.
